text: Book II of the *Republic* carries two arguments, and later readers have often handled them separately. The first builds a city from scratch. Socrates presents it less as political theory than as a way of seeing the soul at a larger scale: the city is the person magnified, the same letters written larger (368c–369a). The second sets rules for what may be said about the gods (379a), and with it Plato entered a quarrel already some two centuries old. Homer and Hesiod were the nearest thing Greece had to scripture, and their gods lied, lusted, fought their own kin, and dealt out good and evil from two jars (379d, quoting *Iliad* 24). The philosopher Xenophanes had mocked those portraits in the sixth century BCE. In 399 BCE an Athenian jury condemned Socrates on charges of impiety and of corrupting the young. Plato's answer is to make the founders of his city theologians before they are lawgivers. They decide what a god must be before they decide what children may hear. The founding premise of the city, that it is a remedy for human neediness, did not go unchallenged. Aristotle would later dispute it and hold that the city is natural to human beings (*Politics* I.2).
